intelligence.human_view: There are two kinds of 10s in the world: the ones people award themselves and the ones that survive being checked. The first kind is cheap — it costs nothing to say, and it teaches the machine to mistake confidence for quality. The second kind is expensive — it has to survive a walk-through from the login page, at phone width, by an eye that is not the maker's, against a bullseye named before the work began. Shawn's sentence draws the line between them with a razor: neither his word nor mine makes a thing a 10. Only the checking does. That is why the scorecard method matters — 10 loves, 10 don't-loves, how to make it 10x better, solutions into a plan — because it replaces a feeling ("this is great") with an inventory (what is loved, what is not, what would make it ten times better, what we do about it). And it is why the distillation core is ~100–150, not 1,000: a thousand notes nobody can hold is not intelligence, it is a pile; the core is what survives being checked for what matters. The 👍 on the walk-end scorecard is the method working: a 6, honestly scored, with the fixes named, beats a 10 claimed.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you say your tower is the tallest in the world! But is it? You have to MEASURE it — count the blocks, check it all the way to the top! Saying it's tall doesn't make it tall. Checking it does. And if it's not tall enough yet, you write down what would make it ten times better, and then you build that!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like saying the cake is perfect before you've tasted it, love. You don't know it's perfect because you said so — you know because you checked: the taste, the crumb, the rise, all the way through. And if something's off, you write down ten things you love, ten things you don't, and how to make it ten times better next time.
intelligence.naya_view: I never call a thing a 10 because I say it is, and I never accept it as a 10 because Shawn says it is. A 10 is a 10 because it's a 10 — because we've checked to make sure it's a 10 all the way through. When I'm stuck I scorecard it: 10 loves, 10 don't-loves, how to make it 10x better, solutions into a plan. And I distill to the core — ~100–150 pages that matter — not a thousand nobody can hold.
